newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican corporates seen extending debt maturities.
newsitem.headline: Mexican corporates seen extending debt maturities.

text.p: A number of Mexican companies with debt coming due will likely try to place longer-term paper, corporate debt analysts said.

Longer-term issues from Mexico and other Latin American sovereign borrowers have paved the way for the longer-term corporate issues in Mexico, they said. And there is a large volume of five-year paper issued in 1992 and 1993 in Mexico that comes due over the next two years.

"I think that most of them will try to do longer maturities, at a minimum to go another five years, but they will do seven or ten if the market will take the paper," said Scott McKee, J.P. Morgan's head of corporate credit research for Latin America.
"Right now, the market is very receptive to longer-dated paper from both Mexico and Argentina," he said.
The Mexican government has placed both a 20-year and a 30-year bond this year. Argentina recently said it will issue a global note maturing in 2006.
Analysts say the pattern is for sovereigns to lead the way, then for high-quality corporates to follow without too much difficulty.

"That is definitely the trend right now, stretching out that yield curve. You do see a lot of this stretching out maturities, going to the Yankee bond market, as opposed to the Eurobond market," said Matthew B. Peck, a corporate bond analyst with Salomon Brothers.
Analysts say Mexican corporate issuers have about $1.53 billion to retire in 1997 and $2.43 billion in 1998.

For instance, retailer El Puerto de Liverpool has a $100 million commercial paper issue coming due this month. Analysts said that the company can easily handle the issue given its excellent financial state. The company is reported to be studying various options.
Holding company Empresas La Moderna is also said to be studying how to best service its $150 million issue that comes due in late 1997.
Analysts add that beverage company Femsa has been talking to banks about refinancing its $300 million issue that comes due in mid-1997.

"Right now we have a lot of these Mexican corporates with short-term debt, one to two years until they mature, so a lot of them are looking to refinance, to restructure their amortization schedules," said Peck.
Both cement maker Cemex SA and broadcaster Grupo Televisa have already restructured debt coming due in the next year or so.
In May, Televisa placed $970 million in notes and debentures to defease $200 million of medium-term notes coming due in November 1997 and for other corporate purposes.
Cemex recently restructured about $1.3 billion of its debt, pushing the maturities out.

"The paper they were assigning in 1995 and in the early part of 1996 was very short-term paper and these companies need to be capitalizing with longer-term paper, and that is their goal, to be longer-term," said Bear Stearns construction analyst Saboni Warner.
Companies may not have specific plans for debt coming due in 1998, but will likely be looking at various alternatives, analysts said.
